region.en: Road to the capital of Videha (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 通往韋提訶王都的大道（象徵定位）

texts.period: Tibetan Kah-gyur (translated c. 9th century), from Indian sources; Schiefner/Ralston translation 1882

source.work: Tibetan Tales Derived from Indian Sources, trans. Schiefner/Ralston (1882), ch. VIII, Mahaushadha and Visakha

summary.en: A traveler feeds at a tank, ties up his meal-pouch without looking, and learns from a soothsayer in the capital that his life is in danger; he cannot remember what prompted the warning until he reaches Mahaushadha, who reasons that the pouch must hold one of the snakes that breathe poison when disturbed - and has him open it with a piece of wood before witnesses: the head rears, the tongue vibrates, and the danger is named.
summary.zh: 旅人在池畔進食，繫袋而不察；至都城中相者告其性命危殆，卻說不出緣由。求教於大藥，大藥推斷袋中必有觸之則吐毒之蛇，命他當眾以木片啟袋——蛇昂首、吐信、怒息噴勃，危險之名由此而定。

sensitivity.note: Kah-gyur narrative literature; living Buddhist tradition treated respectfully.

passages.text: Opening his meal-pouch at the edge of a tank, mixing meal with water and eating, the traveler did not notice the snake that had crept inside while he sat - one of those snakes which emit poison when disturbed. He tied up the pouch unexamined, slung it over his shoulder, and went on to the capital, where a soothsayer told him he was in imminent danger of losing his life.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, Mahaushadha and Visakha (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Regretting that he had not asked on what ground the warning rested, he went not home but to the minister Mahaushadha, who reasoned that the soothsayer must have seen something in the pouch: one of the snakes that breathe poison when disturbed. Bidden to open the pouch with a piece of wood in a retired place before witnesses, the man did so - and when the poisonous snake lifted its head, breathed furiously and made its outstretched tongue vibrate, Mahaushadha said: that is the danger by which you were threatened.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, Mahaushadha and Visakha (1882); not verbatim.

region.en: Villages and hill-towns of Videha (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 韋提訶諸村邑（象徵定位）

texts.period: Tibetan Kah-gyur (translated c. 9th century), from Indian sources; Schiefner/Ralston translation 1882

source.work: Tibetan Tales Derived from Indian Sources, trans. Schiefner/Ralston (1882), ch. VIII, Mahaushadha and Visakha

summary.en: Surveying the land with an army, Mahaushadha finds every village owned by one of the six self-advancing ministers, the king reduced to his own food and drink. His counter-conquest is political, not military: he promises the head-men moderate taxes, tells them to revolt and swear they will submit to no one but Mahaushadha; the king's army cannot take a single hill-town until the first minister rides out, fixes lawful taxes, embraces the people like kin, and reunites all the lands - for which Janaka gives him his daughter.
summary.zh: 大藥巡視疆土，發現六相瓜分全國，國王只剩飲食之權。他不用兵而用政：向各村長許諾減稅安民，教他們叛而聲言「非大藥不服」。王軍連一山寨也攻不下，直到首輔出巡、依法定賦、擁民如親，舉國復歸一統——闍那迦王以女妻之。

sensitivity.note: Kah-gyur narrative literature; living Buddhist tradition treated respectfully.

passages.text: Equipping a complete army to survey the land, Mahaushadha found that whenever he asked to whom the villages, towns and cities belonged, the inhabitants named one minister or another: the six had taken possession of the whole country and King Janaka's rule was restricted to his own food and drink. The king recounted the merciful gods' promise that the son of Purna would recover all his power, and bade Mahaushadha fulfil the deity's words by the force of his intelligence.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, Mahaushadha and Visakha (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Mahaushadha summoned the head-men one after another and promised moderate taxes in place of the immoderate rates levied out of covetousness - but told them first to revolt, and to say they would not submit until the minister Mahaushadha should come. The six ministers went out with a great army and could not get possession of a single village or hill-town; the king could obtain none either, and men fell in battle until all were dejected.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, Mahaushadha and Visakha (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then the inhabitants said: if the first minister Mahaushadha were to come, we would obey him; we have not rebelled against King Janaka, but against ministers who wrought us injury. Riding out at the king's summons, Mahaushadha fixed their taxes according to law, succoured the poor and helpless, greeted and embraced townsfolk and country-folk as if they were his parents and brothers, and the old men, the young and the women looked upon him as a son or a brother. He united all the lands and returned with King Janaka to the seat of royalty - and the king gave his daughter in marriage to him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, Mahaushadha and Visakha (1882); not verbatim.

title.en: No Secret to a Wife: The Peacock Test
title.zh: 秘密不可告妻：孔雀之試

region.en: Court of King Janaka at Videha (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 韋提訶闍那迦王廷（象徵定位）

texts.period: Tibetan Kah-gyur (translated c. 9th century), from Indian sources; Schiefner/Ralston translation 1882

source.work: Tibetan Tales Derived from Indian Sources, trans. Schiefner/Ralston (1882), ch. VIII, Mahaushadha and Visakha

summary.en: Asked at court whom a secret may be trusted to, Mahaushadha answers 'no one, least of all a wife' - and proves it by a staged trap: he hides the king's peacock, eats a double, and shows his wife a courtesan dressed as one of the king's wives. His wife betrays everything to her father, the king orders the minister's execution, and on the road to the cemetery Mahaushadha declaims his famous sloka - a king is no friend, a hangman has no acquaintances, no secret to women, no man should admit to the Brahman's wife Atmavira that he owns a measure of barley - each line a coded confession that untangles the whole plot before the axe falls.
summary.zh: 王問群臣秘密可託何人，大藥答「無人可託，尤不可託妻」，並設局自證：藏起王之孔雀而食其替身，又將一名肖似王妃的妓女引見己妻。妻子果然向父王告密，王遂下令處死首輔。赴刑路上，大藥誦出一首著名的偈頌——國王非友、劊子手無交、秘密勿告婦人、勿向婆羅門之妻阿底摩毘羅承認有麥——五句暗語逐一自白，刀落之前全案冰釋。

sensitivity.note: Kah-gyur narrative literature; living Buddhist tradition treated respectfully.

passages.text: The king asked his ministers to what person a secret might be intrusted: one said a friend, another a wife, a third a mother, a fourth a sister, a fifth a brother. Mahaushadha alone answered that a man ought not to intrust a secret to any one, least of all to his wife - and that he would prove it. He hid the king's missing peacock, cooked and ate another that resembled it, telling his wife to say nothing; then he dressed a courtesan in the likeness of one of the king's wives and introduced her as his mistress.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, Mahaushadha and Visakha (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: His wife, the king's daughter, went straight to her father: the miscreant had sinned against one of the king's wives, eaten the king's peacock, and harbored foreigners. To sift the matter the king ordered his executioners to put Mahaushadha to death; with a karavira wreath on his neck, drum beaten and threats hurled, he was led toward the cemetery, while townsfolk and villagers wept as if a child of their own were being killed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, Mahaushadha and Visakha (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: At the city gate the Brahman's wife Atmavira seized his robe-skirt demanding the measure of barley he had long promised, and Mahaushadha uttered his sloka: 'A king does not become a friend, a hangman has no acquaintances; to women ought no secret to be intrusted; peacock's flesh ought no one to eat; to the Brahman's wife Atmavira a man ought not to admit that he possesses a measure of barley.' Pressed to explain, he unknotted each line: the king he had raised from a king of food and drink to a ruler of the earth; the hangman was the rescued fugitive he had fed and land-granted; the peacock was never eaten, the courtesan was not the king's wife; and the barley line was a rebuke to the woman who dunned a dying man.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, Mahaushadha and Visakha (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: The king placed courtesan and court-lady side by side and found their appearance, figure and behaviour indistinguishable; Mahaushadha was released and heaped with honors. Then he asked the king whether he had learnt what the secrecy of wives is - and, renouncing the king's daughter, went to seek a wife like unto himself in race, beauty, character and wisdom.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, Mahaushadha and Visakha (1882); not verbatim.

title.en: Mahaushadha Wins Visakha of the Kaksha Forest
title.zh: 大藥求婚於迦叉林毘舍佉

region.zh: 迦叉林道旁麥田（象徵定位）

texts.period: Tibetan Kah-gyur (translated c. 9th century), from Indian sources; Schiefner/Ralston translation 1882

source.work: Tibetan Tales Derived from Indian Sources, trans. Schiefner/Ralston (1882), ch. VIII, Mahaushadha and Visakha

summary.en: Disguised as a Brahman ascetic, Mahaushadha seeks a wife as wise as himself and finds a carpenter's daughter in a barley-field who answers every riddle he throws - including pointing him a road while hiding naked at a tank to test whether he recognizes her. Driven off by the village head-men when he proposes clumsily, he learns from her the etiquette of suitors, feasts them properly, and wins her. On the road home he exposes a Brahman's unfaithful wife by pouring barley into a basket with a man hidden inside, buying it at sword's-point price of five hundred gold pieces - and the naked man's father pays to carry off the 'treasure'.
summary.zh: 大藥扮作婆羅門苦行者，在麥田遇木匠之女毘舍佉，屢試其慧皆被妙語化解；她又在池畔赤身藏匿試探他能否相認。初求婚時被村長驅打，她教以求婚之禮，宴請村老而得妻。歸途中他以麥袋試探婆羅門不貞之妻，要將麥倒進藏有情人之籃，逼其以五百金買「藏寶」之籃；裸漢之父倉惶抬籠而去。

sensitivity.note: Kah-gyur narrative literature; living Buddhist tradition treated respectfully.

passages.text: In a barley-field Mahaushadha found a maiden of high race and great modesty. Testing her, he flourished his hands on high while trampling the wheat with his feet; she answered that as his hands flourished on high, so ought his feet. Praised for her earrings and armlets, she said both had little oxen; asked where her father had gone, she said to make two roads out of one by laying thorn-twigs across the road; her mother, to fetch seeds from the fruits of the field.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, Mahaushadha and Visakha (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: She pointed him a crooked road to the Kaksha forest and slipped away to a tank, where she took off her clothes, shut one eye, bowed on one side, and called directions after him - the hand used in eating shows the way. Recognized from afar and greeted in riddling verse, she answered in kind. Driven from the village head-men when he blurted out his proposal - they threatened to have him devoured by fierce dogs - he was coached by the maiden herself in the order of wooing: draw near, gain favor, give hospitality and organize an entertainment, and only then bring forward the desire. So he feasted the head-men and won her.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, Mahaushadha and Visakha (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: On the road home a Brahman's wife refused him shelter - and admitted another man. When her husband returned she hid her visitor in a basket; pressed to pour his barley into that same basket, she invented one excuse after another until, terrified, she sent for the lover's father, who bought the 'treasure' basket for five hundred gold pieces and had it carried off by a strong man. Mahaushadha lighted a lamp beside the basket and let them go.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, Mahaushadha and Visakha (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: He paid a hundred gold pieces to warn the householder about his wife's character, and sent the remaining four hundred to Visakha with a missive revealing his true name: chief minister of the king of Videha, no Brahman, come only to carry out his quest. When the delivering Brahman handed over three hundred of the pieces, Visakha looked under the bed at once - 'men have come from the court with orders to seize the malefactor' - and caught him by driving a peg into the clay she asked him to test his foot in, holding him for the fourth hundred.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, Mahaushadha and Visakha (1882); not verbatim.
